2023B-p1#c: The claim concerns every integer assignment, not a fixed finite grid. Start with the polynomial's finite total degree and choose a sufficiently large finite set of integers.
Apply Schwartz–Zippel on a grid whose side length exceeds that degree. If the polynomial vanished at every grid point, its zero probability would be one, contradicting the bound.
Mention the underlying characteristic-zero field and total degree. A polynomial can vanish on a small finite grid without being the zero polynomial.
2024C-p1#b: Compare the size of the proposed coordinate set with the total degree. You need existence of one nonzero evaluation, not nonzeroness at every point.
Sample every coordinate independently from that set. The zero-probability bound is strictly below one, so some grid point must have nonzero value.
State why probability strictly below one gives existence. Check that the listed field elements are distinct in the underlying field.
2025B-p1#a: This is a univariate polynomial question. Count how many distinct roots are being demanded relative to its degree.
A nonzero univariate degree-d polynomial has at most d distinct roots. Verify the number of distinct roots of unity under the question's field assumptions, then compare.
Do not confuse ‘roots of the equation’ with only primitive roots of exactly that order. Use the meaning intended by the statement.
2024A-p6#x: Write a general member of the span as a linear combination with symbolic coefficients, then take its determinant.
If the span contains an invertible matrix, this determinant polynomial is not identically zero. Its total degree is at most the matrix dimension. Evaluate a random combination and test invertibility.
Prove both cases and the one-sided error direction. Include the cost of forming the combination and computing its determinant.
2025A-p5#x: Name the difference of the two symbolic determinants as one polynomial. Equality becomes a zero-polynomial question.
Bound the determinant difference's degree by the matrix dimension. Assign shared edge variables consistently in both graphs, evaluate both determinants, and compare their values.
Using different random values for the same variable in the two determinants would invalidate the test. State the failure probability and arithmetic or bit-cost model.
2025C-p4#x: For each branching program, express the accepted-path sum as the designated entry of its layer-matrix product. Subtract the two outputs.
Bound degree using the number of layers and label degrees. Evaluate the same random variable assignment in both programs and multiply the numerical matrices instead of expanding all paths.
Explain why the matrix entry equals the program polynomial and why evaluation is polynomial time. Bound error using total degree, not the number of paths.
2023A-p5#x: Suppose the best completion has rank r. Then some r-by-r minor is nonzero under that completion; fix that minor for the analysis.
Its symbolic determinant is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most r. Randomly fill the unknown entries, compute rank, and bound the chance this fixed witness minor becomes zero.
You need not enumerate all minors or union bound over them. Prove the returned rank cannot exceed the optimum, and account for repeated variables if entries are linked.
hw2026s1-p2#x: Begin with leaves and the problem's exact convention for formula size. The statement must be compatible with a single variable leaf.
At an addition node, use the larger child degree. At a multiplication node, add child degrees and compare with the size of the parent tree.
Treat constants and the zero polynomial consistently. Do not reuse this argument for circuits with shared subexpressions without changing the size analysis.
hw2026s1-p1#x: Induct on the number of variables. Regard the polynomial as a univariate polynomial in the last variable whose coefficients are polynomials in the others.

Separate the event that its leading coefficient vanishes from the event that the resulting nonzero univariate polynomial vanishes. The coefficient's degree plus the last-variable degree is at most the total degree.
Do not apply the univariate root bound when every specialized coefficient is zero. Handle that event with the inductive hypothesis and then combine the bounds.
hw2026s1-p4#x: Parameterize the matrix span by one variable per input matrix. Invertibility is detected by the determinant of that symbolic combination.
Prove that a single invertible combination makes the determinant polynomial nonzero. Randomly choose coefficients from a sufficiently large field subset and check the resulting numerical rank.
Give the sampling-set size, error direction and cost of constructing the matrix. A zero determinant on one sample is not a certain ‘no’ certificate.
hw2026s1-p5#x: Place distinct variables on a diagonal matrix between the two given matrices in a product whose determinant is defined.
Expand by Cauchy–Binet. Each size-n index set gives a distinct squarefree monomial with coefficient equal to the product of its two minors. Nonzero coefficients correspond exactly to common bases.
Check dimensions and transpose placement. Distinct monomials avoid cancellation between different index sets; nonzero minors on both sides are necessary.
hw2025s1-p4#x: Choose one fingerprinting approach and define exactly what Alice sends. A polynomial fingerprint lets a bit string become coefficients of a univariate polynomial.
Use a shared or transmitted random evaluation point in a field of size larger than the degree by the needed error factor. Bob evaluates his string at the same point and compares fingerprints.
Count bits for both the evaluation point and field value, specify how the field is agreed upon, and prove equal strings never disagree while unequal ones collide only with the bounded probability.
2025C-p1#a: Translate being a root of unity into an equation and write the larger exponent as an integer multiple of the smaller one.
Raise the smaller-power identity to the quotient exponent. If the wording means exact multiplicative order, distinguish dividing the larger order from having exactly that larger order.
State which meaning of ‘order-k root’ is being used. Being a root of the larger unity equation does not imply being primitive of the larger order.
2023A-p6#x: Build two coefficient arrays with a one at each input-set element and zero elsewhere. Ask what the coefficient at a target sum counts.
Multiply the two polynomials. Every pair contributes once at the exponent equal to its sum; positive coefficients identify the sumset. Choose padding beyond the maximum possible sum.
Explain both membership and representation counts. Runtime depends on the numeric universe bound, not just the number of elements in the sets.
2024B-p2#x: Split the input vector in half and write the two output halves using the four blocks of the Hadamard matrix.
Compute the two smaller transforms once each, then obtain the output halves by their sum and difference. Do not recursively recompute a transform for every block occurrence.
Use vector dimension in the recurrence and translate from the matrix's index if necessary. Include the scalar base case.
2025A-p1#b: Track the degree of each intermediate power, not just the number of multiplications. The final coefficient vector can be much longer than the original one.
Use repeated squaring with FFT products. Their lengths grow geometrically, so summing their actual costs can avoid an unnecessary extra logarithmic factor.
State the degree of the input polynomial from the question and the arithmetic-cost model. Do not price every product at the smallest input size.
2025B-p4#x: Evaluation changes polynomial multiplication into pointwise multiplication. Locate the assumption in the question that the divisor does not vanish at the chosen roots of unity.

Evaluate both polynomials by FFT at those roots, divide corresponding values to get quotient values, then apply the inverse FFT. The stated quotient degree bound makes these values sufficient for unique recovery.
Cite the nonvanishing assumption before dividing. Give the quotient degree bound and count the two evaluations, pointwise divisions and interpolation in the runtime.
hw2026s2-p5#x: Multiply the stated block matrix by a vector split into two halves. Write the resulting pair of vector expressions.
Reuse two recursive transforms and combine them by elementwise addition and subtraction. The number of entries touched at this level is linear in the vector length.
Check signs in both output halves, the base case, and whether the matrix index denotes dimension or its logarithm.
hw2025s3-p2#a: You already have the two direct products. Expand the product of the two sums of halves and locate the two cross terms.
Subtract the known direct products from this one extra multiplication. The remainder is exactly the cross-term sum needed for recombination.
Count multiplications separately from additions. Do not compute either cross product individually after obtaining their sum.
hw2025s3-p2#b: Use part (a)'s multiplication count as the number of recursive children. Identify the work spent on additions and recombination.
The recurrence has three half-size calls and linear local work. Compare the linear exponent with the exponent determined by three children and a halving factor.
State a constant-size base case and include carries if this is integer multiplication. The exponent comes from the number of recursive products, not the number of cross terms.
hw2025s3-p1#x: After multiplication, determine the largest exponent of the first variable. The substitution base must exceed that value so exponent pairs cannot collide.
Encode an exponent pair as a mixed-radix integer exponent using the stated substitution. Multiply the resulting univariate polynomials, then recover each pair by quotient and remainder.
Check collision-freedom for product degrees, not only input degrees. Bound the encoded degree and decoding cost.
hw2025s3-p3#x: Place indicator coefficients at elements of the two sets. Write one coefficient of their product as a sum over index pairs.
Every product of two one-coefficients corresponds to a representation of that exponent as a sum. Read all requested counts from one FFT product.
Specify the universe size, sufficient padding and exact integer recovery if discussing numerical FFT implementation. Presence and number of representations are different outputs.
2014A-p6#x: Split each binary integer into high and low halves using a power of two as the base. Expand the product symbolically.
Replace the two cross multiplications by a product of sums minus the direct products. Recombine using shifts and additions, then write the resulting recurrence.
Sums of halves can gain one bit; mention why this does not change the exponent. Count bit operations for additions and shifts under the required model.
2023A-p1#d: Think of each four-by-four matrix as a two-by-two matrix of two-by-two blocks.
Apply Strassen at the block level, then again inside each small block product. Multiply the number of block products by the scalar multiplications per block.
The question counts multiplications, not all arithmetic operations. Distinguish a block multiplication from a scalar multiplication.
2024A-p1#b: A nonnegative determinant constrains the product of eigenvalues. Could two negative eigenvalues have a positive product?
Try a small diagonal symmetric matrix with two negative diagonal entries. Compute both its determinant and its quadratic form at a coordinate vector.
Verify symmetry and the determinant hypothesis, then exhibit a negative quadratic form. An unexplained matrix example is not a complete counterexample.

Apply Gaussian elimination or incremental independence tests, then Gram–Schmidt on the independent vectors. Skip zero residuals rather than dividing by their norm.
Handle dependent input vectors and distinguish arithmetic operations from exact representation of square roots if the complexity model asks for bit lengths.
2024C-p2#x: Compare one Boolean product entry with the corresponding ordinary integer product entry for zero–one inputs.

Use integer arithmetic or a modulus too large for positive counts to become zero. Multiplication modulo two computes parity, not Boolean OR.
2025A-p1#c: Place all the input vectors side by side as columns of a single matrix. What are the columns of its product with the given matrix?
Compute the whole collection of matrix–vector outputs by one fast matrix–matrix multiplication, then extract columns.
Include construction and output costs and compare the resulting exponent with three. Independent naive matrix–vector computations are not a lower bound.
2025B-p1#b: Partition the wide right-hand matrix into square blocks of the same width as the left-hand matrix.
Multiply the left matrix by each square block and concatenate the outputs. Count the number of square products and multiply by their fast-multiplication cost.
Check dimensions and the output-size cost. Explain why the final exponent is strictly below the naive one.

A reachable vertex has a simple path of length at most one less than the vertex count. Use repeated Boolean squaring, thresholding after products, to capture all such paths without huge path counts.
Prove both directions of reachability and state how the zero-length diagonal convention is handled. Include the logarithmic number of matrix products.

Expand the formal product of the linear factors using eigenvalues. The coefficient corresponding to the requested degree gives the answer up to a known sign; the product of all eigenvalues is the determinant.
Track sign and dimension carefully. Do not assume the eigenvalues must first be computed numerically.
2024B-p4#x: For a candidate distance, express ‘every ordered pair has a path of at most this length’ using a power of the adjacency matrix with self-loops.

Use the strong-connectivity assumption for a finite search range. Count products per test and number of tests; prevent integer path-count blowup by Boolean thresholding.
2025C-p1#b: Partition each large matrix into a square array of smaller blocks. Apply the smaller multiplication scheme at the block level.

Check the model of multiplication algorithms: a scalar procedure using divisions or commutativity cannot automatically be lifted to noncommuting blocks. State the bilinear/block-compatible assumption used.
hw2026s2-p4#x: Use self-loops to make exact-length powers represent bounded-length reachability. Begin from the adjacency relation rather than enumerating paths.
Repeatedly square in the Boolean sense until the represented length covers every simple path. Each Boolean product can use an ordinary nonnegative product followed by thresholding.
Bound both the number of squarings and entry magnitudes after thresholding. Explain why a positive entry cannot represent a nonexistent path.
hw2025s2-p4#x: Expand a diagonal entry of the cube of the adjacency matrix. It counts closed walks of length three starting at that vertex.

State the graph assumptions and multiplicity explicitly. Count the matrix multiplications and the final trace computation.

Raise this relation to a sufficiently large power by repeated squaring. Interpret nonzero entries and use Boolean thresholding to keep intermediate counts controlled.
Justify the exponent from the longest needed simple path, and count all matrix multiplications. Clarify whether diagonal reachability is included.
hw2025s3-p5#a: Prove equality of kernels first rather than comparing ranks directly. One inclusion follows immediately by multiplying by the transpose.
For the other inclusion, multiply the equation involving the Gram matrix on the left by the vector's transpose. A squared real norm equal to zero forces the original matrix–vector product to vanish.

hw2025s3-p5#b: Diagonalize the symmetric matrix and ask how many diagonal coordinates can map nontrivially.
Similarity by an invertible orthogonal matrix preserves rank. The diagonal matrix's rank counts its nonzero eigenvalues, including multiplicities.
Distinguish algebraic from geometric multiplicity and state why symmetry makes them equal. Use the actual matrix dimension in the subtraction.
hw2025s3-p5#c: Combine the previous kernel result with the characteristic polynomial of the Gram matrix. Which coefficient reveals the multiplicity of the zero root?
Compute that polynomial using the permitted parallel routine, then find the smallest exponent with a nonzero coefficient. Subtract the zero-root multiplicity from the column dimension.
Give parallel depth and processor/work bounds for matrix formation, characteristic polynomial and coefficient selection. Handle the all-zero matrix.
hw2025s3-p6#a: Take an eigenvector and insert it into the defining quadratic-form inequality.
Use the eigenvector equation to rewrite the quadratic form as the eigenvalue times a strictly positive squared norm. Infer the sign of the eigenvalue.
State real symmetry so the eigenvalues and eigenvectors in this argument have the required properties. The eigenvector must be nonzero.
hw2025s3-p6#b: Write an orthogonal diagonalization and use part (a) to take real square roots of its diagonal eigenvalues.
Choose a factor formed from the square-root diagonal matrix and the transpose of the eigenvector matrix. Multiply its transpose by itself to verify the factorization.
Check the order of factors; reversing them can give the wrong matrix. Zero eigenvalues are allowed and do not require inverses.

Reassociate the expression as the squared norm of the factor times the vector. This is nonnegative for every real vector; also check symmetry of the product.
Prove the claim for every vector, not only basis vectors. The factor need not be invertible or square.

Write seven half-size recursive calls plus quadratic local work. Compare the resulting master-theorem exponent with two.
Include a base case and report the tight bound under the stated arithmetic model. Do not confuse Strassen's seven products with classical multiplication's eight.

Work in characteristic two, where minus one and plus one coincide. Each nonzero permutation term corresponds to one perfect matching, so the determinant gives the count's parity.
Use the bipartite adjacency matrix and compute over the field with two elements. A zero determinant here means even parity, not necessarily absence of a perfect matching.
